claims.text: Slow cooling during HfNbTaTiZr composite solidification increases elemental segregation.
Rapid quenching minimizes segregation and produces a comparatively homogeneous HfNbTaTiZr microstructure.
Elemental segregation produces microstructural regions having distinct thermal expansion coefficients.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between heterogeneous regions generates internal thermal stresses during cooling and subsequent heating.
Segregation can increase elastic stresses between distinct solid-solution regions.
Internal thermal stresses modify dislocation mobility.
Internal thermal stresses modify phase stability.
Stress-induced changes in dislocation dynamics and phase stability alter the alloy's elastic response.
Stress-induced changes in dislocation dynamics and phase stability alter plastic deformation and high-temperature creep.
Slow-cooled, more strongly segregated samples will have higher residual internal stresses than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled, more strongly segregated samples will have higher room-temperature microhardness than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow cooling and enhanced segregation will alter the temperature dependence of the elastic moduli.
Slow cooling and enhanced segregation will modify high-temperature creep behavior, potentially including activation energy or strain-rate sensitivity.
The standard as-cast HfNbTaTiZr initial state has minimal elemental segregation.
Relevant HfNbTaTiZr creep behavior occurs at 1250 °C.
Relevant HfNbTaTiZr elastic-modulus behavior spans 293–1100 K.
The proposed segregation-driven thermal-stress mechanism provides a unified explanation for the reported creep, hardness, and thermoelastic-modulus phenomena.
The proposed controlled comparison uses slow-cooled samples and rapidly quenched samples as the baseline control.
